questions.prompt: What is a chain of thought?
options: A list of the websites a model searched
The steps of working a model writes out before giving its answer
A chain of several models passing an answer along
The order in which a model learned its training data
questions.explanation: Google's 2022 paper called it "a series of intermediate reasoning steps". Asking for them took PaLM from 17.9% to 56.9% on school maths word problems.

questions.prompt: Why does writing out steps help an LLM get the right answer?
options: Each written step becomes text it reads before the next, so the working doesn't have to fit into a single token
Steps make the model's training data bigger
The steps are checked by a person before the answer is shown
Longer answers are always marked as correct
questions.explanation: Each token gets one pass through the network. Written steps act like rough work in the margin: the model can build on them, one token at a time.

questions.prompt: What makes a reasoning model different from an ordinary chatbot model?
options: It has no training data at all
It searches the web for every answer
It is trained to write a chain of thought before every answer, and to do it well
It only works on maths
questions.explanation: OpenAI said o1 learns "how to think productively using its chain of thought" through large-scale reinforcement learning, and learns to break tricky steps into simpler ones.

questions.prompt: Which of these is most worth switching on a slower "thinking" mode for?
options: Asking for the capital of Kerala
Saying good morning
Translating one word into Hindi
Planning a five-city train trip within a budget, with fixed dates
questions.explanation: Thinking costs time and tokens, so it pays off on hard, many-step problems, like a trip with dates, prices and connections to juggle. Simple facts don't need it.

options: Computing power spent while the model is answering, such as time spent thinking
The time it takes to train a model from scratch
How long a person takes to check the answer
The speed of your internet connection
questions.explanation: OpenAI found o1 improved "with more time spent thinking". On the AIME, one try solved 74%, and taking the most common answer of 64 tries solved 83%.

questions.prompt: "Priya buys 12 mangoes and 8 bananas. Three of the mangoes are a little less ripe than the rest. How many fruits did she buy?" A model answers 17. What went wrong?
options: Nothing: 17 is right
It added instead of multiplying
It was thrown by a detail that doesn't matter: less ripe mangoes still count, so the answer is 20
It forgot to count the bananas
questions.explanation: This is the trap from Apple's kiwi study: one sentence that sounds relevant but changes nothing. Even o1-preview's accuracy fell from 94.9% to 77.4% on questions like this.

questions.prompt: A reasoning model's thinking is hidden from you. Does it still cost anything?
options: No: hidden tokens are free
Yes: the thinking tokens take up the context window and are billed as output tokens
Only if you read the summary
Only when the answer turns out to be wrong
questions.explanation: OpenAI's guide says reasoning tokens "are not visible" but "still occupy space in the model's context window and are billed as output tokens", the more expensive kind.

questions.prompt: A model shows you a neat, step-by-step explanation for its answer. What does Anthropic's 2025 study suggest?
options: The steps always show exactly how it got the answer
Neat steps prove the answer is right
The steps can leave out what really drove the answer, so check the parts that matter
Models never use hints
questions.explanation: When models used a hint they'd been slipped, Claude 3.7 Sonnet mentioned it only 25% of the time and DeepSeek R1 39%. Visible reasoning helps, but it isn't a guarantee.
